title: Bengal's Shakta and Vaishnava streams
hook: a goddess shaped from river clay, welcomed home like a daughter, and sent back to the river

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bengal's Shakta and Vaishnava streams, through Chaitanya, singing the names of Krishna humbler than a blade of grass. Did you let someone else be right? Day one thousand three hundred seventy-nine, the end of a week.

Straw, bound tight with twine into the shape of a body. Then clay from the riverbank, pressed on in layers, smoothed by thumbs, left to dry, cracked, filled, smoothed again. Day after day, in workshops along the river in Bengal. Slowly a face appears: wide eyes, a calm mouth, many arms, a lion at her feet. Then paint, cloth, jewelry. By autumn she's ready, and families and neighborhoods carry her in. Today, the Shakta stream at its most public, Durga Puja, and the question of what happens to her at the end.
screen: `STRAW AND RIVER CLAY.` → `A FACE APPEARS.` → `CARRIED IN, IN AUTUMN.`

segments.voice: The text behind Durga is the Devi Mahatmya, and it tells of her as a warrior: the gods pour their powers into her, she rides out on her lion, and she defeats the buffalo demon none of them could. That's the image in the clay, spear in hand. But in Bengal, the festival tells a second story at the same time. Durga is also Uma, the daughter of the mountain king Himalaya and his wife Menaka. She's married to Shiva and lives far away on his mountain, and once a year she comes home to visit her parents, bringing her children. Turn it once. So the festival feels like a homecoming. Bengali songs, called agamani, the songs of arrival, put words in the mother's mouth: is my Uma really coming? How thin has she gotten? What has that husband of hers been feeding her? In Bengal, the fierce goddess and the daughter whose mother worries about her are one. Turn it again. On the last day, Vijaya, she has to go back. Married women, in a custom called sindur khela, smear red vermilion on the goddess's face and on each other, the way you'd send a daughter off. And then the image, all that patient work, is carried to the river and lowered into the water, and the clay goes back where it came from. The goodbye songs are sad, and the greeting afterward is happy: people visit, embrace, share sweets. And here's the week behind us: Sambandar's song at the temple tank, Kannappa's eye, Tirumular's cows, the conch and the drum, Ramprasad's ledger, Chaitanya's street. Now a goddess who comes home, and goes.
screen: `THE WARRIOR ON THE LION` · `UMA, THE DAUGHTER COMING HOME` · `RED VERMILION FOR GOODBYE` · `THE CLAY GOES BACK TO THE RIVER`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: welcome and farewell. Sit, and let the breath slow. On the in-breath, think of someone you love arriving: the door opening, their face. Let yourself be glad. On the out-breath, think of letting them go again: the door closing, the car pulling away. Don't hold on to either. Just breathe the arriving and the leaving, in and out, for the whole sit. If you pray, you can hold that person before the Goddess, or before God, as they come and as they go. The bell holds the time.
Bengal's Shakta and Vaishnava streams. Today, Durga Puja: the warrior goddess welcomed home as Uma, the daughter, then given back to the river. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: Bengal's Shakta and Vaishnava streams. Today, when someone arrives or leaves, give the moment its full weight: a real welcome, a real goodbye. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: At Durga Puja, Bengali Hindus install clay images of Durga in homes and neighborhood pavilions, worship her for the festival days, and on Vijaya Dashami immerse the image in a river or pond.
